narrative:
The model determined that you have a 96% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school uses this prediction to decide admissions, your application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily against you were your class ranking in your third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year class ranking. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure.

Your third-year ranking placed you at the very bottom of your class (decile 1), far below the average ranking of about 6 among students who were accepted. This was the single biggest reason the model expected you to struggle on the bar. Your LSAT score of 24 was also well below the average of 37 seen in successful applicants, adding further weight toward a failing outcome. Finally, your first-year ranking (also decile 1) continued in the same low direction, though it had less influence than the later ranking and test score.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude you were very likely to fail the bar, making admission too risky for the school.

What you should do next is focus on improving your substantive legal knowledge and test-taking skills. Consider retaking the LSAT, seeking targeted bar-prep tutoring, or enrolling in a program with strong academic support before reapplying. Strengthening these core areas can meaningfully change your future predictions. (218 words)
